title: Misinformation on salt water use among Nigerians during 2014 Ebola outbreak and the role of social media
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 703 Nigerians asking whether they received the (false) message that salt water prevents or treats Ebola during the 2014 outbreak, and through which channel. It reports self-reported receipt of a specific piece of misinformation as a share of respondents with a stated denominator (95.02%, 668/703; 37.41%, 263/703 via social media), which is a RECALL-exposure estimate.

estimates.platform: Any channel (family, friends or social media) - self-reported receipt, survey administered online
estimates.date: Survey fielded 5 August 2017 to 6 August 2018; respondents recalled the 2014 Ebola outbreak
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported receiving a message telling them to use salt water for protection against Ebola during the 2014 outbreak
estimates.value_raw: Yes 668, 95.02% (of 703); reported in text as 95.02% and in the abstract as 95.0%
estimates.denominator: 703 members of the general Nigerian population who were in Nigeria during the 2014 Ebola outbreak and returned an analysable online questionnaire
estimates.definition: Answered 'Yes' to having received information/a message to use salt water for protection against Ebola during the outbreak period; no threshold or frequency scale, a simple yes/no
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given. The single false claim is named in the Introduction: "Misinformation on the use of salt water for Ebola prevention and treatment had gone viral in Nigeria, and had even led to adverse consequences for some users"
estimates.source_quote: Almost all of them reported having received some information to use salt water for protection against Ebola during the period of the outbreak (95.02%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 177, text and Table 2 ('Received information to use salt: Yes 668, 95.02')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Coded self_report because the construct is RECALL: the respondent reports the encounter and nothing external verifies it. Note however that the researchers, not the respondent, established falsity - they pre-specified one known-false claim (salt water prevents/treats Ebola) and asked only whether it had been received, so the respondent made no veracity judgement of their own. Exposure rests on unverified self-report a full three years after the events. No coder reliability applies.
estimates.moderator_quote: A cross-sectional study was conducted among the general Nigerian population who were in Nigeria during the 2014 Ebola outbreak. Around a thousand invitations to the survey (on Google forms) were sent out via 3 social media platforms (WhatsApp, Facebook and e-mail) from the 5th of August, 2017 to the 6th of August, 2018.
estimates.notes: Recall window is the whole 2014 outbreak, asked in 2017-2018, so recall error is likely large and one-directional questions ('did you receive...') invite acquiescence. ground_truth is coded self_report per the RECALL convention, but note the asymmetry: the respondent judged only receipt, while the researchers fixed which claim counted as misinformation. That makes this a sharper measure than an open-ended 'have you seen fake news?' item, and the moderator field alone does not show it. The sample is a self-selected online convenience sample, overwhelmingly male (73.8%), tertiary-educated (97.3%), north-western (64.7%) and drawn heavily from medical and health occupations (~46%), so it is not representative of Nigeria.

estimates.platform: Social media (platform not specified in the item)
estimates.date: Survey fielded 5 August 2017 to 6 August 2018; respondents recalled the 2014 Ebola outbreak
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents whose source of the salt-water-for-Ebola message was social media
estimates.denominator: 703 members of the general Nigerian population who were in Nigeria during the 2014 Ebola outbreak and returned an analysable online questionnaire (Table 2's 'Source of information' block totals 703)
estimates.definition: Named 'social media' rather than family or friends as the source of the message instructing them to use salt water against Ebola
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given. The single false claim is named in the Introduction: "Misinformation on the use of salt water for Ebola prevention and treatment had gone viral in Nigeria, and had even led to adverse consequences for some users"
estimates.source_quote: The predominant source of this message was the social media (37.41%).
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, p. 177; restated in the abstract as '37.4% of whom received such message on social media'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: As above: self-reported receipt and self-reported channel; the falsity of the salt-water claim was designated by the authors, not judged by the respondent.
estimates.moderator_quote: The predominant source of this message was the social media (37.41%).
estimates.notes: Confidence medium for two reasons. (1) The abstract phrases this as '37.4% of whom', implying a denominator of the 668 who received a message, but Table 2's source block sums to 703 (207+204+263+29), so the printed 37.41% is 263/703 - i.e. the table's denominator silently readmits the 34 respondents who said they received no message. I have kept the verbatim 37.41% and recorded the 703 denominator that reproduces it. The Table 2 block is not quotable as a contiguous span, so the source_quote is the prose restatement on p. 177. (2) Respondents could name only one source, so this is a first/main-source attribution, not the share who ever saw the claim on social media, which will be higher.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately not extracted: (1) '24%' who used salt water and the sub-splits of how (drinking 40%, bathing 47%, both 13%) - acting on misinformation is a behavioural outcome, not exposure, sharing or content prevalence. (2) 'Initial reaction: Accept 424, 60.31%' - that is belief in a false claim, explicitly out of scope. (3) 'Received contrary information: Yes 300, 42.67%' - exposure to CORRECTIVE information, the mirror image of what the review measures. (4) 'Attempted to verify: Yes 358, 50.92%' - a verification behaviour. (5) Figure 3 (how often they believe health information on social media: almost always 11%, sometimes 49%, rarely 32%) - a belief disposition toward social-media health information in general, not toward misinformation. (6) Figure 4 (how often they share health information received on social media: never 22%, rarely 38%, ... almost always 7%) - this is sharing of health information IN GENERAL, with no falsity condition attached, so it is not a misinformation-sharing recall estimate; had the item been restricted to false content it would have been a RECALL-sharing row. (7) Table 3's salt-water-use breakdowns by demographic and by information source are subgroup analyses of the behavioural outcome, not of exposure. (8) The Introduction's '38.3% of tweets contained medically correct information' and '95% of 400 Nigerian youths were on at least one social media platform' are figures cited from other studies - barred by R8. Minor internal inconsistency noted: the abstract says 73.2% male, Table 1 gives 519/703 = 73.83%.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms) of the general Nigerian population who were in Nigeria during the 2014 Ebola outbreak. About 1,000 invitations distributed via WhatsApp, Facebook and e-mail between 5 August 2017 and 6 August 2018; 760 questionnaires retrieved (stated response rate 76.0%), 57 grossly incomplete dropped, 703 analysed. Bilingual (English/Hausa) 22-item instrument covering demography, receipt of the salt-water message, its source, salt-water use and reasons, and belief/sharing of social-media health information. Analysis by descriptive statistics, chi-square and multivariate logistic regression (SPSS 22). No pilot, validity or reliability statistics reported; no coding of content, so no inter-rater statistics apply. Self-selected convenience sample, skewed male (73.8%), tertiary-educated (97.3%), north-western (64.7%) and health-professional; retrospective recall of events three years earlier; ethics approval YSSH/DTR/GEN/302.
rob.item6_quote: The survey questionnaire contained 22 items with questions on socio-demography, receipt of information/messages regarding salt water use for Ebola prevention, whether they had used salt water or not and why, and how frequently they believed or shared health information they received on social media.
rob.item10_quote: A total of 760 questionnaires were retrieved, giving a response rate of 76.0%. Fifty seven out of these were grossly incomplete thus, further analyses were restricted to the remaining 703 questionnaires. ... Almost all of them reported having received some information to use salt water for protection against Ebola during the period of the outbreak (95.02%).
